notes.front: What is a software development lifecycle (SDLC) model?
notes.back: A simplified, big-picture description of how software gets built: which phases and activities happen, and how they connect in logic and in time.
notes.explanation: The syllabus holds that testing has to be adapted to whichever SDLC a team follows if it is to succeed.
notes.example: Like the method section of a recipe, but for building software: it says which steps come first and how later ones depend on them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a sequential development model?
notes.back: An SDLC model that works through its phases one after another, so executable code usually appears only in the later phases.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names the waterfall model and the V-model as examples, and notes that code usually comes late in such models.
notes.example: Like building a house: foundations, then walls, then roof, with nobody living in it until the end.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an iterative development model?
notes.back: An SDLC model that develops the software through a series of repeated cycles (iterations); the spiral model and prototyping are examples.
notes.explanation: In some such models each iteration is expected to deliver a working prototype, so the product is revisited again and again.
notes.example: Like drafting an essay several times, each draft a full pass that is reworked in the next.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an incremental development model?
notes.back: An SDLC model that delivers the product as a series of increments; the Unified Process is the syllabus’s example.
notes.explanation: In some incremental models each iteration is assumed to deliver a working product increment that can be tested.
notes.example: Like opening a new shop one department at a time: groceries first, then clothing, then electronics.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a test level?
notes.back: “A specific instantiation of a test process.”
notes.explanation: Each test level is its own occurrence of the test process.
notes.example: Like the separate inspections of a new car: engine on the bench, then the assembled car on the road.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test level”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A specific instantiation of a test process.

notes.front: What is a test type?
notes.back: “A group of test activities based on specific test objectives aimed at specific characteristics of a component or system.”
notes.explanation: A test type is defined by its test objectives and the characteristics of the component or system it targets.
notes.example: Like grouping a car’s checks by what they examine (brakes, fuel economy, comfort) rather than by when they happen.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test type”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A group of test activities based on specific test objectives aimed at specific characteristics of a component or system.

notes.front: What is component testing?
notes.back: “A test level that focuses on individual hardware or software components.”
notes.explanation: Its focus is on individual components, taken one at a time.
notes.example: Like testing a single light switch on the bench before it is wired into a house.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “component testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test level that focuses on individual hardware or software components.

notes.front: What is integration testing?
notes.back: “A test level that focuses on interactions between components or systems.”
notes.explanation: The definition covers interactions between components and between systems; the syllabus treats these as two separate levels.
notes.example: Like checking that the switch actually turns on the lamp once both are wired together.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “integration testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test level that focuses on interactions between components or systems.

notes.front: What is component integration testing?
notes.back: “The integration testing of components.”
notes.explanation: It narrows integration testing to the joins between components inside one system.
notes.example: Like checking that a shopping basket module hands the right totals to the checkout module in the same app.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “component integration testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is system testing?
notes.back: “A test level that focuses on verifying that a system as a whole meets specified requirements.”
notes.explanation: The key words are “as a whole”: it looks at the complete system against its specified requirements.
notes.example: Like test-driving a finished car against its specification sheet, rather than testing its parts.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “system testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test level that focuses on verifying that a system as a whole meets specified requirements.

notes.front: What is system integration testing?
notes.back: “A test level that focuses on the integration of systems.”
notes.explanation: Where component integration testing looks inside one system, this level looks at how separate systems work together.
notes.example: Like checking that a shop’s website and its separate warehouse system agree on stock levels.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “system integration testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test level that focuses on the integration of systems.

notes.front: What is acceptance testing?
notes.back: “A test level that focuses on determining whether to accept the system.”
notes.explanation: Its focus is a decision: whether the system should be accepted.
notes.example: Like a buyer’s final walk-round of a new flat before signing that the work is complete.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “acceptance testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test level that focuses on determining whether to accept the system.

notes.front: What is functional testing?
notes.back: “A test type to determine the functional suitability of a test object.”
notes.explanation: It is a test type, so it can be aimed at a test object at any level; its target is functional suitability.
notes.example: Like checking that a coffee machine really makes the drinks on its menu, not how quickly it makes them.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “functional testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test type to determine the functional suitability of a test object.

notes.front: What is non-functional testing?
notes.back: “A test type to evaluate that a component or system complies with non-functional requirements.”
notes.explanation: Its yardstick is the non-functional requirements of the component or system.
notes.example: Like timing how long the coffee machine takes per cup and how loud it is, once you know it makes coffee.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “non-functional testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test type to evaluate that a component or system complies with non-functional requirements.

notes.front: What is black-box testing?
notes.back: “A test approach based on the specification of a component or system.”
notes.explanation: The tester works from what the item is specified to do, without needing to see inside it.
notes.example: Like testing a calculator app only from its user guide, never opening its code.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “black-box testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test approach based on the specification of a component or system.

notes.front: What is white-box testing?
notes.back: “A test approach based on the internal structure of a component or system.”
notes.explanation: It is the counterpart of black-box testing: the tests come from how the item is built.
notes.example: Like reading the calculator app’s code and making sure every branch of its rounding logic is run by some test.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “white-box testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test approach based on the internal structure of a component or system.

notes.front: What is confirmation testing?
notes.back: Change-related testing done after a defect is fixed, to confirm that the failure the defect caused does not happen again.
notes.explanation: It is triggered by a specific fix and looks back at that one defect’s failure.
notes.example: Like re-trying the exact door that stuck, after the locksmith says it is repaired.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “confirmation testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A type of change-related testing performed after fixing a defect to confirm that a failure caused by that defect does not reoccur.

notes.front: What is regression testing?
notes.back: Change-related testing that checks whether defects have been introduced, or uncovered, in parts of the software that were not changed.
notes.explanation: Its attention is on the unchanged areas, where a change can have unintended effects.
notes.example: Like checking the other doors and windows still lock after the locksmith has worked on one door.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “regression testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A type of change-related testing to detect whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software.

notes.front: What is impact analysis?
notes.back: Working out which parts of the software a change could affect.
notes.explanation: The syllabus advises doing it before regression testing, so the extent of that testing can be judged.
notes.example: Like tracing which rooms share a pipe before turning off the water to fix one tap.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is maintenance testing?
notes.back: “A test type that evaluates the effect of changes made to an operational system or its environment.”
notes.explanation: The system is already in operation, so the testing is about the effect of a change, including changes to its environment.
notes.example: Like checking a live payroll system after its database server is moved to new hardware.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “maintenance testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test type that evaluates the effect of changes made to an operational system or its environment.

notes.front: In maintenance, what is a hot fix?
notes.back: An unplanned release or deployment of a change to an operational system.
notes.explanation: The syllabus contrasts planned releases with unplanned ones, and calls the unplanned ones hot fixes.
notes.example: Like an emergency patch pushed on a Saturday night because customers cannot log in.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is test-driven development (TDD)?
notes.back: A development approach where test cases steer the coding: tests come first, and code is written until they pass.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says the test cases take the place of extensive up-front software design in steering the code.
notes.example: Like writing the exam questions before the lesson, then teaching until every question can be answered.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is behavior-driven development (BDD)?
notes.back: A development approach that writes an application’s intended behaviour as plain-language test cases that stakeholders can read and agree.
notes.explanation: Because the test cases are in plain language, people outside the development team can read and agree them.
notes.example: Like a restaurant agreeing each dish with the customer in plain words (“arrives hot, no nuts”) before the kitchen cooks it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the Given/When/Then format?
notes.back: The simple natural-language format in which BDD test cases are usually written.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names it as the usual way BDD keeps its test cases easy for stakeholders to understand.
notes.example: Given a basket holding two books, When the shopper removes one, Then the basket shows one book.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is DevOps?
notes.back: An organisational approach that turns development (testing included) and operations into one joint effort with shared goals.
notes.explanation: The aim, in the syllabus’s account, is synergy between two functions that are often kept apart.
notes.example: Like a restaurant where cooks and waiting staff plan the evening together instead of passing plates through a hatch.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is continuous integration (CI), as the syllabus presents it?
notes.back: A technical practice promoted by DevOps; the syllabus says it pushes developers to hand in good code with component tests and static analysis attached.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names it as one of the practices that let DevOps teams build, test and release good code faster.
notes.example: Like a newsroom where every reporter files each paragraph as it is written, and a checker runs over it at once, rather than all copy arriving at midnight.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is continuous delivery (CD), as the syllabus presents it?
notes.back: A DevOps technical practice, paired with CI, that helps teams build, test and release code faster through a delivery pipeline.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists it beside CI among the practices DevOps promotes, and rates it even better than CI for shifting testing left.
notes.example: Like a bakery conveyor that takes each loaf from oven to shelf with checks on the way, instead of a weekly bulk delivery.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is shift left?
notes.back: “A test approach to perform testing and quality assurance activities as early as possible in the software development lifecycle.”
notes.explanation: The approach is about timing: testing and quality assurance activities are moved as early as possible in the lifecycle.
notes.example: Like proof-reading each chapter as it is drafted instead of only proof-reading the finished book.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “shift left”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test approach to perform testing and quality assurance activities as early as possible in the software development lifecycle.

notes.front: What is a retrospective?
notes.back: A meeting where the people involved look back on a stretch of work to decide what to keep, what to improve and how.
notes.explanation: The syllabus presents retrospectives as a mechanism for process improvement, including of testing.
notes.example: Like a sports team reviewing the last match together before planning the next training week.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus, to succeed, testing must be {{c1::adapted to the SDLC}} that the project follows.
notes.explanation: No single way of testing fits every lifecycle; the lifecycle sets the conditions testing works under.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An SDLC model shows how development phases and activities relate to each other in which two ways?
notes.back: Logically and chronologically (in time).
notes.explanation: A model says both what depends on what and what happens when.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council’s new permit system is specified in full, then designed, then coded over nine months, and only then handed to testers to run. Which kind of SDLC model is this?
notes.back: A sequential development model
notes.choices:
A) A sequential development model
B) An iterative development model
C) An incremental development model
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing is repeated in cycles; each phase happens once. C: the system is not delivered in increments; it arrives in one piece at the end.
notes.explanation: Phases in strict order, with code appearing only late, is the pattern of a sequential model.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team builds a rough mock-up of a booking app, shows it to users, reworks it and shows it again, several times over. Which SDLC model is the team following?
notes.back: Prototyping, an iterative development model
notes.choices:
A) Prototyping, an iterative development model
B) The V-model, a sequential development model
C) The waterfall model, a sequential development model
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: both sequential models pass through each phase once and do not rework a mock-up in repeated cycles.
notes.explanation: Repeated build-show-rework cycles are what the syllabus files under iterative models, with prototyping as a named example.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A project follows the Unified Process. In the syllabus’s terms, which family of SDLC model is that?
notes.back: Incremental
notes.choices:
A) Incremental
B) Sequential
C) It is an Agile practice, not an SDLC model
notes.choicesExplained: B: the syllabus’s sequential examples are the waterfall model and the V-model. C: the syllabus lists the Unified Process among SDLC models, not among methods and Agile practices.
notes.explanation: The syllabus places the Unified Process under incremental development models.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides TDD and BDD, what are two development methods or Agile practices the syllabus names?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: Scrum, Kanban, extreme programming, domain-driven design, feature-driven development.
notes.explanation: The syllabus gives a longer list of examples; these are all on it, and so is acceptance test-driven development.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1 “Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two aspects of testing that the choice of SDLC affects?
notes.back: Any two of: scope and timing of test activities; detail of test documentation; test techniques and approach; extent of automation; the tester’s role.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists five such aspects, which is why testing has to be adapted to the lifecycle.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team moves from a waterfall project to Scrum, and its 80-page test specifications shrink to short checklists on a wiki. Which impact of the SDLC on testing does this show?
notes.back: The level of detail of test documentation.
notes.explanation: The lifecycle change alters how much test documentation is written, one of the five impacts the syllabus lists.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On one project a tester can only run tests in the last two months; on another, every test level runs in each two-week iteration. Which SDLC impact explains the difference?
notes.back: The scope and timing of test activities (such as which test levels run, and when).
notes.explanation: The lifecycle decides when testing can happen and what it covers at each point.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After switching to an Agile lifecycle, testers stop designing every test in advance and rely more on experience-led exploration. Which SDLC impact is this?
notes.back: The choice of test techniques and test approach.
notes.explanation: How tests are derived is one of the aspects of testing the syllabus says the lifecycle affects.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm that used to release twice a year starts releasing every week and builds a large automated regression suite. Which SDLC impact on testing is this?
notes.back: The extent of test automation.
notes.explanation: How much testing is automated is one of the aspects that the chosen lifecycle drives.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester who used to receive finished builds from another department now joins the product team from the first planning session. Which SDLC impact on testing is this?
notes.back: The role and responsibilities of a tester.
notes.explanation: What a tester does, and when they are involved, changes with the lifecycle.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a sequential development model, what do testers typically do in the early phases?
notes.back: Reviewing requirements, and carrying out test analysis and test design.
notes.explanation: These activities need documents, not running code, so they fit the early phases.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why can dynamic testing typically not be done early in a sequential development model?
notes.back: The executable code is usually created only in the later phases.
notes.explanation: Dynamic testing needs something to run; the syllabus keeps the hedge “usually” for when code appears.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Month two of a twelve-month V-model project: requirements exist, but no code does. Which task can the tester usefully do now?
notes.back: Review the requirements and start test analysis and design
notes.choices:
A) Review the requirements and start test analysis and design
B) Run the system tests
C) Execute the regression suite
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: both need executable code, which in a sequential model usually arrives only in the later phases.
notes.explanation: In the early phases of a sequential model, testers typically work on reviews, analysis and design.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In iterative and incremental models where each iteration delivers a working increment, what testing may be done in every iteration?
notes.back: Both static and dynamic testing, at all test levels.
notes.explanation: A working increment exists each time round, so there is something to run as well as something to review.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does frequent delivery of increments require from testing?
notes.back: Fast feedback and extensive regression testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus ties both needs to how often increments are delivered.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team ships a new increment every two weeks, but its manual regression checks take three weeks to run. Which need of frequent delivery is it failing to meet?
notes.back: Fast feedback with extensive regression testing
notes.choices:
A) Fast feedback with extensive regression testing
B) Detailed up-front test documentation
C) Dynamic testing only in the final phase
notes.choicesExplained: B: frequent delivery calls for speed, not heavier documentation. C: testing only at the end is the sequential pattern, not what increments need.
notes.explanation: Frequent increments need regression results faster than the increments arrive.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Given that change may come at any time, which two things do Agile projects favour?
notes.back: Slim work-product documents, plus heavy test automation that eases regression testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus links both to the assumption that change may occur throughout the project.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Agile projects, which kind of test technique does most manual testing tend to use?
notes.back: Experience-based test techniques, which need little detailed test analysis and design in advance.
notes.explanation: The syllabus keeps the hedge: most manual testing “tends to” work this way.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a Scrum team, a manager asks for a 150-page test specification to be finished before each sprint starts. What does the syllabus say Agile projects favour instead?
notes.back: Slim work-product documents, supported by heavy test automation.
notes.explanation: Agile development expects change throughout, so heavy documents written in advance would keep going stale.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.1 “Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under the good practices for every SDLC, what should each software development activity be paired with?
notes.back: A matching test activity, so that no development activity escapes quality control.
notes.explanation: The pairing means no piece of development escapes some form of checking.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.2 “Software Development Lifecycle and Good Testing Practices”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why should different test levels have specific and different test objectives?
notes.back: So that, between them, the levels cover enough ground without duplicating each other’s work.
notes.explanation: Distinct objectives let each level cover its own ground, so together they are thorough without repeating one another.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.2 “Software Development Lifecycle and Good Testing Practices”, p. 25
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When should test analysis and design for a given test level begin?
notes.back: In the matching development phase, so that testing keeps to the principle of early testing.
notes.explanation: Waiting until the matching code exists would push this work later than it needs to be.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.2 “Software Development Lifecycle and Good Testing Practices”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When should testers start reviewing work products?
notes.back: As soon as drafts of them are available.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says this earlier testing and defect detection supports shift left.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.2 “Software Development Lifecycle and Good Testing Practices”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company only starts designing its system tests after all the code is written, although the system requirements were finished months earlier. Which good practice is it missing?
notes.back: Beginning test analysis and design during the corresponding development phase
notes.choices:
A) Beginning test analysis and design during the corresponding development phase
B) Giving each test level different objectives
C) Automating all regression tests
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing here says the levels share objectives. C: automation is not one of the syllabus’s four good practices for every SDLC.
notes.explanation: System test design could have begun alongside the system requirements work, following the principle of early testing.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the order of the three steps in TDD?
notes.back: Write the tests; write code that satisfies them; refactor the tests and code.
notes.explanation: Tests come first by design; refactoring comes only once the code passes.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer writes a discount-calculation function, then adds unit tests for it the next day. Is that TDD?
notes.back: No: in TDD the tests are written before the code
notes.choices:
A) No: in TDD the tests are written before the code
B) Yes: any code with unit tests is TDD
C) Yes, as long as the code is refactored afterwards
notes.choicesExplained: B: having tests is not enough; the order matters. C: refactoring is only the final step of a sequence that starts with the tests.
notes.explanation: The defining feature of TDD is that the tests come first and direct the coding.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In BDD, what should happen to the natural-language test cases?
notes.back: They should be translated automatically into executable tests.
notes.explanation: The plain-language cases then serve both as agreed behaviour and as tests that can be run.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester sees: “Given a user with an expired card, When they pay, Then the payment is declined.” With which approach does the syllabus link this format?
notes.back: BDD
notes.choices:
A) BDD
B) TDD
C) CI
notes.choicesExplained: B: the syllabus describes TDD by its test-first order, not by a natural-language format. C: CI is a delivery practice, not a test-case format.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says BDD test cases usually use the Given/When/Then format.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: TDD, acceptance test-driven development and BDD each implement which testing principle, and why?
notes.back: Early testing, and so shift left, since each test exists before the code it checks.
notes.explanation: Writing tests before code is by definition testing earlier in the lifecycle.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of development model do test-first approaches such as TDD and BDD support?
notes.back: An iterative development model.
notes.explanation: The syllabus places these approaches alongside iterative development rather than a single long pass.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What may the tests written in TDD, acceptance test-driven development or BDD become once the feature is built?
notes.back: Automated tests that persist, protecting code quality through later changes and refactoring.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “may”: the tests can be kept and rerun, not that they always are.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team writes its acceptance tests for a new loyalty-points feature before any code for it exists. Is that an example of shift left?
notes.back: Yes. Defining tests before the code is written applies early testing, which is shift left.
notes.explanation: The syllabus gives exactly this reason for counting test-first approaches as shift left.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.3 “Testing as a Driver for Software Development”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does DevOps require of an organisation’s culture?
notes.back: A change of culture that closes the gap between development (testing included) and operations, valuing both functions equally.
notes.explanation: Tools alone do not close the gap; the syllabus calls for a change in how the groups regard each other.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two things DevOps promotes?
notes.back: Any two of: team autonomy, fast feedback, integrated toolchains, and technical practices such as CI and CD.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says these let teams build, test and release good code faster through a delivery pipeline.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Developers at a bank hand each release to a separate operations group and move on; the operations group has no say in what is built. What does DevOps aim to change here?
notes.back: To bridge development (including testing) and operations so they work together towards common goals, valued equally.
notes.explanation: The hand-over wall is exactly the gap the syllabus says DevOps tries to close.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does CI promote shift left in testing, according to the syllabus?
notes.back: It pushes developers to hand in good code with component tests and static analysis attached.
notes.explanation: Checks travel with each submission, so problems surface as the code arrives rather than later.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where CI is used, what does the syllabus call good practice for regression testing?
notes.back: Including automated regression tests in it.
notes.explanation: Each integration can then re-check existing behaviour automatically.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Each time a developer pushes code, component tests and static analysis go with it and results come back within minutes. Which DevOps technical practice is at work?
notes.back: Continuous integration
notes.choices:
A) Continuous integration
B) A retrospective
C) A sequential development model
notes.choicesExplained: B: a retrospective is a meeting to improve the process, not a code-submission practice. C: a sequential model is an SDLC model, not a DevOps practice.
notes.explanation: Submitting code with component tests and static analysis is how the syllabus describes CI promoting shift left.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Among the practices for achieving shift left, how does the syllabus rate CD compared with CI?
notes.back: It ranks CD even higher than CI, citing fast feedback and automated component tests that go with each code submission.
notes.explanation: Both practices appear on the shift-left list; the syllabus singles CD out as the stronger of the two.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants every change to travel through an automated pipeline that builds, tests and readies it for release. Which practice promoted by DevOps does this describe?
notes.back: Continuous delivery
notes.choices:
A) Continuous delivery
B) Prototyping
C) A retrospective
notes.choicesExplained: B: prototyping is an iterative SDLC model, not a pipeline practice. C: a retrospective is an improvement meeting.
notes.explanation: The syllabus links CD with a delivery pipeline that lets teams build, test and release faster.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which DevOps benefit for testing concerns whether a change harms existing code?
notes.back: Fast feedback on code quality and on whether changes adversely affect existing code.
notes.explanation: Frequent automated checks tell the team quickly when something that worked has broken.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus, what do automated processes like CI/CD make easier to establish for testing?
notes.back: Stable test environments.
notes.explanation: The syllabus counts this among the testing benefits of automated CI/CD processes.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under DevOps, which kind of quality characteristics become more visible?
notes.back: Non-functional quality characteristics.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists this increased visibility among the benefits of DevOps for testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does automation through a delivery pipeline reduce the need for?
notes.back: Repetitive manual testing.
notes.explanation: Checks that are the same every time can be left to the pipeline.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why is the risk of regression minimised in DevOps?
notes.back: Because of the scale and range of the automated regression tests.
notes.explanation: The more automated regression tests run, and the wider they reach, the smaller the regression risk.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Since adopting a DevOps pipeline, a team’s testers no longer spend Fridays repeating the same login and search checks by hand. Which DevOps benefit is this?
notes.back: Automation reduces the need for repetitive manual testing
notes.choices:
A) Automation reduces the need for repetitive manual testing
B) Stable test environments are no longer needed
C) Manual testing is no longer needed at all
notes.choicesExplained: B: the syllabus says automated processes help establish stable environments, not that environments stop mattering. C: the syllabus says manual testing, especially from the user’s perspective, is still needed.
notes.explanation: Removing repeated hand checks is the pipeline benefit the syllabus names.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which DevOps risk or challenge concerns the delivery pipeline itself?
notes.back: The pipeline must be defined and established.
notes.explanation: The benefits depend on a pipeline that someone first has to design and build.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which DevOps challenge concerns CI/CD tools?
notes.back: They must be introduced and maintained.
notes.explanation: Tools are an ongoing commitment, not a one-off purchase.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What challenge does test automation bring in DevOps?
notes.back: It needs extra resources and may be hard to establish and maintain.
notes.explanation: The syllabus keeps the hedge “may”: automation is not always hard, but it can be.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A start-up adopts DevOps, but nobody is given time to look after its automated test suite, which soon breaks and is abandoned. Which DevOps challenge did it meet?
notes.back: Test automation needs extra resources and can be hard to maintain
notes.choices:
A) Test automation needs extra resources and can be hard to maintain
B) DevOps removes the need for a delivery pipeline
C) DevOps forbids manual testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: a pipeline must be defined and established; DevOps does not remove it. C: the syllabus says manual testing is still needed.
notes.explanation: Unresourced automation decays, which is the risk the syllabus names.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does a high level of automated testing in DevOps remove the need for manual testing?
notes.back: No. People still need to test by hand, above all from the user’s point of view.
notes.explanation: Automation covers repeated checks, but the syllabus still expects people to test as users would.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A director proposes cutting all manual testing because the new DevOps pipeline is fully automated. Does the syllabus support this?
notes.back: No. However much is automated, people still need to test by hand, above all from the user’s point of view.
notes.explanation: The syllabus treats user-perspective manual testing as something DevOps does not replace.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.4 “DevOps and Testing”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which testing principle is sometimes referred to as shift left?
notes.back: The principle of early testing.
notes.explanation: Shift left is the name for performing testing earlier in the SDLC.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A testing lead moves test-case writing from the week before release to the week the requirements are agreed. Which test approach is this?
notes.back: Shift left
notes.choices:
A) Shift left
B) Regression testing
C) Maintenance testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: regression testing checks unchanged areas after a change; nothing has changed here. C: maintenance testing concerns changes to a system already in operation.
notes.explanation: Moving testing activities as early as possible in the lifecycle is the glossary definition of shift left.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “shift left”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test approach to perform testing and quality assurance activities as early as possible in the software development lifecycle.

notes.front: Which shift-left practice looks at specifications from a tester’s point of view, and what does it often find?
notes.back: Testers review the specification from their own angle; this often exposes potential defects such as ambiguous, incomplete or inconsistent statements.
notes.explanation: Problems in a specification can be caught before any code is built on top of them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which shift-left practice involves a test harness during implementation?
notes.back: Writing test cases before the code exists, then running the code in a test harness as it is built.
notes.explanation: The code is exercised against its tests from the moment it starts to exist.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does static analysis of source code count as a shift-left practice?
notes.back: By running it on the source code ahead of dynamic testing, or automatically within a pipeline.
notes.explanation: Static analysis needs no running system, so it can be done ahead of dynamic tests.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why is non-functional testing at the component test level a form of shift left?
notes.back: Non-functional tests tend to be done late, once a complete system and representative environment exist; starting at component level moves them earlier.
notes.explanation: The syllabus adds “where possible”: not every non-functional test can start at component level.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer times how long a single pricing component takes to handle 10,000 prices, weeks before the full system exists. Which shift-left practice is this?
notes.back: Non-functional testing starting at the component test level
notes.choices:
A) Non-functional testing starting at the component test level
B) Reviewing the specification from testers’ perspective
C) Confirmation testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing is being reviewed; a component is being run and timed. C: confirmation testing checks a defect fix, and no fix is involved.
notes.explanation: Timing is a non-functional check, done here at component level instead of waiting for the full system.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before coding starts, a tester reads the user stories for a parking app and asks what “near the entrance” means in metres. Which shift-left practice is she applying?
notes.back: Reviewing the specification from testers’ perspective
notes.choices:
A) Reviewing the specification from testers’ perspective
B) Static analysis of source code
C) Using continuous delivery
notes.choicesExplained: B: there is no source code yet to analyse. C: continuous delivery concerns submitted code and pipelines, not reading stories.
notes.explanation: Spotting an ambiguity in a specification is the kind of potential defect this practice often finds.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Shift left brings testing forward; it is no licence to {{c1::neglect}} the testing done later in the SDLC.
notes.explanation: Early testing adds to later testing; the syllabus is explicit that it does not replace it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Having adopted shift left, a team proposes dropping system testing altogether because “we test early now”. Is that in line with the syllabus?
notes.back: No. Shift left adds early testing; it does not make later testing, such as system testing, something to drop.
notes.explanation: Some checks still need the complete system; shift left adds early testing on top.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What cost trade-off does the syllabus describe for shift left?
notes.back: It may need extra training, effort or cost early on, but is expected to save effort or cost later.
notes.explanation: The saving is “expected”, not guaranteed; the syllabus hedges it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.5 “Shift Left”, p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When are retrospectives often held?
notes.back: Typically when a project, an iteration or a release milestone ends, and at any other time one is needed.
notes.explanation: They are tied to natural pause points, but can also be called when a need arises.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the syllabus say must happen to improvements recommended in a retrospective?
notes.back: They must be followed up.
notes.explanation: The syllabus calls retrospectives critical to continuous improvement, which only happens if agreed changes are carried out.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team holds a lively retrospective every sprint, but the same three problems appear on the board each time and nothing changes. What is it neglecting?
notes.back: Following up the recommended improvements.
notes.explanation: Without follow-up, retrospectives cannot deliver the continuous improvement they exist for.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which retrospective question looks at what went well?
notes.back: What worked, and should be kept?
notes.explanation: Successes are named so they are kept, not just problems fixed.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which retrospective question looks at what went badly?
notes.back: What did not work, and could be done better?
notes.explanation: The question is framed towards improvement rather than blame.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which retrospective question looks forward to the next piece of work?
notes.back: How will we build in the improvements, and keep the successes, next time?
notes.explanation: It turns the first two questions into action for what comes next.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where are the results of a retrospective normally recorded?
notes.back: In the test completion report.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says results “should be recorded” and are “normally” part of that report.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: At the end of a release, a test manager wants the retrospective’s conclusions kept with the release’s testing records. Where would the syllabus normally expect them?
notes.back: In the test completion report
notes.choices:
A) In the test completion report
B) In the requirements specification
C) Nowhere; retrospective results are not recorded
notes.choicesExplained: B: the requirements are not where test-process lessons are kept. C: the syllabus says the results should be recorded.
notes.explanation: Retrospective results are normally part of the test completion report.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After a retrospective, a team acts on a suggestion to prepare test data the day before each run, and its test runs now finish a day sooner. Which typical retrospective benefit is this?
notes.back: Increased test effectiveness or efficiency.

notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a retrospective, testers and developers go through the team’s test process together and agree to rewrite its unclear test procedures. Which typical benefit is this?
notes.back: Increased quality of testware.
notes.explanation: Jointly reviewing how testing is done leads to better test products.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A new tester says the retrospective was the first time she felt able to raise a concern and suggest a fix, and she learned how others work. Which typical benefit is this?
notes.back: Team bonding and learning.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a retrospective, testers point out that many user stories lacked acceptance criteria, and the product owner agrees to add them in future. Which typical benefit is this?

notes.front: Each sprint, a team’s retrospective looks at how developers and testers hand work to each other, and hand-offs have become smoother. Which typical benefit is this?
notes.back: Better cooperation between development and testing.
notes.explanation: Regularly reviewing how the two groups collaborate lets them improve it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.1.6 “Retrospectives and Process Improvement”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between a test level and a test type?
notes.back: A level groups testing by stage of development (component up to system); a type groups it by the quality characteristics tested.
notes.explanation: The two are independent dimensions: most types can be done at any level.
notes.contrast: Level answers “at what stage and scope?”; type answers “testing for what?”.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2 “Test Levels and Test Types”, p. 28
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is non-functional testing a test level or a test type?
notes.back: A test type
notes.choices:
A) A test type
B) A test level
C) A review type
notes.choicesExplained: B: the five test levels run from component testing to acceptance testing. C: review types are forms of static testing such as inspections.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names non-functional testing among its four test types.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In sequential SDLC models, how are test levels often chained together?
notes.back: Each level’s exit criteria are built into the entry criteria of the level that follows it.
notes.explanation: One level has to be finished to an agreed standard before the next begins.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the five test levels, in the syllabus’s order?
notes.back: Component testing, component integration testing, system testing, system integration testing, acceptance testing.
notes.explanation: The scope widens from a single component to accepting the system for use.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In version 4.0 of the syllabus, what happened to the single integration testing level?
notes.back: It became two levels of its own: component integration testing and system integration testing.
notes.explanation: This is why the syllabus counts five test levels rather than four.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, Appendix C “Release Notes”, p. 75
