notes.front: Which of these is not one of the syllabus’s five test levels?
notes.back: Regression testing
notes.choices:
A) Regression testing
B) Component integration testing
C) Acceptance testing
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: both are among the five test levels the syllabus describes.
notes.explanation: Regression testing is change-related testing that can happen at any level; it is not a level itself.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What other name is component testing also known by in the syllabus?
notes.back: Unit testing.
notes.explanation: The two names are used interchangeably for testing components on their own.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does component testing focus on, according to the syllabus?
notes.back: Testing components in isolation.
notes.explanation: Other components are kept out of the picture, which is what separates this level from component integration testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of support does component testing often require?
notes.back: Special tooling, for example test harnesses or unit test frameworks.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names test harnesses and unit test frameworks as examples of such support.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who normally performs component testing, and where?
notes.back: Developers, in their development environments.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “normally”: it is the usual arrangement, not a rule.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer uses a unit test framework to check a postcode-validation function on its own, on her laptop. Which test level is this?
notes.back: Component testing
notes.choices:
A) Component testing
B) System testing
C) Acceptance testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: system testing looks at the whole system’s behaviour, not one function. C: acceptance testing is about accepting the system, ideally by its intended users.
notes.explanation: One component, in isolation, with a framework, in the developer’s own environment: every marker of component testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What other name does the syllabus give component integration testing?
notes.back: Unit integration testing.
notes.explanation: It mirrors component testing’s other name, unit testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does component integration testing focus on?
notes.back: The interfaces and interactions between components.
notes.explanation: The target is where components meet, not each component alone.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is component integration testing heavily dependent on?
notes.back: The integration strategy, such as bottom-up, top-down or big-bang.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “heavily dependent”, naming bottom-up, top-down and big-bang as example strategies.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester checks that an app’s basket module passes the correct item totals to its checkout module. Which test level is this?
notes.back: Component integration testing
notes.choices:
A) Component integration testing
B) System integration testing
C) Component testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: both modules are inside one app; no external system is involved. C: two components are being tested together, not one in isolation.
notes.explanation: The target is the interaction between two components of the same system.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does system testing focus on, according to the syllabus?
notes.back: How the whole system or product behaves and what it can do, taken as one complete unit.
notes.explanation: The scope is the entire system or product, not its parts.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two kinds of testing does system testing often include?
notes.back: End-to-end functional tests of whole tasks, and non-functional tests of qualities such as usability.
notes.explanation: With the whole system present, complete tasks and overall qualities can both be checked.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who may perform system testing, and what is it related to?
notes.back: An independent test team can do it, and it works from the system’s specifications.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “may”: an independent team is an option, not a requirement.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An independent test team runs complete “search, book and pay” journeys on a finished holiday-booking app in an environment set up like production. Which test level is this?
notes.back: System testing
notes.choices:
A) System testing
B) Component integration testing
C) Acceptance testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the team is testing whole journeys on the complete system, not interfaces between components. C: acceptance testing is aimed at deciding whether to accept the system, ideally by intended users; here an independent test team checks behaviour.
notes.explanation: End-to-end tasks on the entire system, by an independent team, in a representative environment, all point to system testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does system integration testing focus on?
notes.back: Where the system under test connects with other systems and outside services: its interfaces with them.
notes.explanation: The target is the boundary between the system under test and what lies outside it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of test environment does system integration testing require?
notes.back: A suitable one, preferably similar to the operational environment.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “preferably” similar to the operational environment, not identical to it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester checks that a clinic’s appointment system sends correct booking details to an outside text-message service. Which test level is this?
notes.back: System integration testing
notes.choices:
A) System integration testing
B) Component integration testing
C) Component testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the interface is with an external service, not between components of one system. C: more than one component is involved, across two systems.
notes.explanation: Interfaces between the system under test and an external service are the focus of system integration testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does acceptance testing focus on, according to the syllabus?
notes.back: Validation, and demonstrating readiness for deployment: that the system meets the user’s business needs.
notes.explanation: Where system testing checks against specifications, acceptance testing asks whether the system is fit for its users’ business.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Ideally, who should perform acceptance testing?
notes.back: The intended users.
notes.explanation: “Ideally” is the syllabus’s word, so other arrangements also occur.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before signing off a new stock-control system, warehouse staff use it for a week on their real daily tasks to check it meets their needs. Which test level is this?
notes.back: Acceptance testing
notes.choices:
A) Acceptance testing
B) System testing
C) System integration testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: system testing checks the system against its specifications, and may be done by an independent test team, not by users judging business needs. C: no interface with another system is being tested.
notes.explanation: Intended users validating that the system meets their business needs before deployment is acceptance testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are three of the main forms of acceptance testing the syllabus lists?
notes.back: Any three of: user acceptance testing; operational; contractual; regulatory; alpha testing; beta testing.
notes.explanation: All are forms within the one acceptance testing level, not separate levels.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus, where does beta testing belong?
notes.back: It is a form of acceptance testing
notes.choices:
A) It is a form of acceptance testing
B) It is a separate sixth test level
C) It is a test type
notes.choicesExplained: B: the syllabus has five test levels, and beta testing is listed within acceptance testing. C: the syllabus’s four test types are functional, non-functional, black-box and white-box.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists alpha and beta testing among the main forms of acceptance testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two attributes the syllabus uses to distinguish test levels?
notes.back: Any two of: test object; test objectives; test basis; defects and failures; approach and responsibilities.
notes.explanation: The syllabus calls this list non-exhaustive, so other attributes can also be used.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Component tests at a firm are run by developers, while acceptance tests are run by the customer’s staff. Which attribute distinguishing test levels does this difference fall under?
notes.back: Approach and responsibilities.
notes.explanation: Who carries out the testing, and how, is part of what makes each level distinct.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: One test level derives its tests from a module’s detailed design; another derives them from the customer’s business process descriptions. Which distinguishing attribute differs?
notes.back: The test basis.
notes.explanation: What the tests are derived from is one of the attributes that separate the levels.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between component integration testing and system integration testing?
notes.back: Component integration testing tests interfaces between components of one system; system integration testing tests interfaces with other systems and external services.
notes.explanation: Both are integration testing, but at different boundaries.
notes.contrast: Inside the system versus at its edge.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does system testing differ from acceptance testing in focus?
notes.back: System testing checks the whole system’s behaviour and capabilities against its specifications; acceptance testing validates readiness for deployment against users’ business needs.
notes.explanation: The same complete system is tested, but against different yardsticks.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.1 “Test Levels”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the four test types the syllabus addresses?
notes.back: Functional testing, non-functional testing, black-box testing and white-box testing.
notes.explanation: Two pairs: what is tested (functions versus other characteristics) and where tests come from (specification versus structure).
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus’s shorthand, functional testing is about “what” the test object should do. What does it evaluate?
notes.back: The functions the component or system is meant to carry out.
notes.explanation: Functions are the things the system is meant to do, as opposed to how well it does them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the main objective of functional testing check?
notes.back: Functional completeness, functional correctness and functional appropriateness.
notes.explanation: These three together make up whether the functions are all there, right and fit for purpose.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester checks that a mortgage calculator returns the right monthly payment for a given loan and rate. Functional or non-functional testing?
notes.back: Functional testing
notes.choices:
A) Functional testing
B) Non-functional testing
C) Neither; it is maintenance testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing about speed or other qualities is being checked; the question is whether the function gives the right answer. C: no change to an operational system is involved.
notes.explanation: Checking what the function does, and that its results are correct, is functional testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus’s shorthand, non-functional testing checks what about the system?
notes.back: “How well the system behaves”: attributes other than its functional characteristics.
notes.explanation: It sets aside whether a function exists and asks about qualities such as speed or security.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester measures whether a ticketing site still responds within three seconds when 5,000 people try to buy at once. Functional or non-functional testing?
notes.back: Non-functional testing
notes.choices:
A) Non-functional testing
B) Functional testing
C) Confirmation testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the tester is not checking what the site does, but how well it behaves under load. C: no defect fix is being checked.
notes.explanation: Response time under load is about how well the system behaves.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two of the non-functional quality characteristics the syllabus lists?
notes.back: Any two of: performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability, safety.
notes.explanation: These are the eight characteristics in the classification the syllabus uses.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of these is not one of the syllabus’s non-functional quality characteristics?
notes.back: Traceability
notes.choices:
A) Traceability
B) Compatibility
C) Safety
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: compatibility and safety are both in the syllabus’s list of eight.
notes.explanation: Traceability links test products to their basis; it is not a quality characteristic of the product in this list.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester checks how much memory and time an image-resizing service uses per picture. Which quality characteristic is under test?
notes.back: Performance efficiency
notes.choices:
A) Performance efficiency
B) Portability
C) Security
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing is being moved to another platform. C: no protection against misuse is being checked.
notes.explanation: Time and resource use are what performance efficiency is about.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester tries to read other patients’ records by changing a number in a web address. Which characteristic is under test?
notes.back: Security
notes.choices:
A) Security
B) Compatibility
C) Maintainability
notes.choicesExplained: B: the question is not whether the system works alongside others. C: ease of changing the code is not being assessed.
notes.explanation: Trying to reach data one should not see tests how well the system protects it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Five first-time users are timed and observed while trying to book a doctor’s appointment on a new app, and their confusion is noted. Which characteristic is under test?
notes.back: Usability
notes.choices:
A) Usability
B) Reliability
C) Portability
notes.choicesExplained: B: the question is not whether the app keeps working over time. C: no change of platform is involved.
notes.explanation: How easily real users can get their task done is a usability concern.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: By what other name does the syllabus say usability is also known?
notes.back: Interaction capability.
notes.explanation: The syllabus gives both names so learners recognise either.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: By what other name does the syllabus say portability is also known?
notes.back: Flexibility.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists both names side by side, so a question may use either.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is it ever appropriate to start non-functional testing early in the SDLC?
notes.back: Sometimes, yes: for example as part of reviews or component testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “sometimes”; not all non-functional testing can start early.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How are many non-functional tests derived from functional tests?
notes.back: They reuse the functional tests but also check that a non-functional constraint is met while the function runs.
notes.explanation: The same steps serve twice: once for what happens, once for how well.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can the late discovery of non-functional defects do to a project?
notes.back: Pose a serious threat to its success.
notes.explanation: The syllabus stresses “late”: the threat comes from when such defects are found.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team already has a functional test that exports a report. It reruns the same test while also checking the export finishes within ten seconds. What has it done?
notes.back: Derived a non-functional test from a functional one, by adding a check on a non-functional constraint.
notes.explanation: The function is exercised as before; the extra check is on how well it performs.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where does black-box testing derive its tests from?
notes.back: From documents describing what the test object should do, not how it is built inside; it is specification-based.
notes.explanation: The tester needs to know what the item should do, not how it is built.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the main objective of black-box testing?
notes.back: Seeing whether the system behaves as its specifications say it should.
notes.explanation: The specification is the yardstick, so differences from it are what the tests find.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where does white-box testing derive its tests from?
notes.back: From how the system is built: its code, architecture, work flows and data flows.
notes.explanation: It is structure-based, so the design of the tests follows how the thing is built.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the main objective of white-box testing?
notes.back: To exercise enough of the underlying structure with tests to reach an acceptable level of coverage.
notes.explanation: Success is measured by how much of the structure the tests exercise.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester writes tests for a parking-fee calculator using only its published tariff table. Black-box or white-box testing?
notes.back: Black-box testing
notes.choices:
A) Black-box testing
B) White-box testing
C) Both equally
notes.choicesExplained: B: the tester never looks at the code or internal structure. C: nothing in the tests comes from the structure.
notes.explanation: Tests from a specification, with no regard for internal structure, are black-box tests.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer reads the parking-fee calculator’s code and adds tests until every one of its if-statements has been exercised both ways. Black-box or white-box testing?
notes.back: White-box testing
notes.choices:
A) White-box testing
B) Black-box testing
C) Acceptance testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the tests come from the code, not from a specification. C: acceptance testing is a test level about accepting the system, not a way of deriving tests from code.
notes.explanation: Deriving tests from the code’s structure and aiming to cover it is white-box testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between functional and non-functional testing?
notes.back: Functional testing checks what the system should do; non-functional testing checks how well it behaves.
notes.explanation: A function can be present and correct yet too slow or insecure, which only non-functional testing would reveal.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 29
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between black-box and white-box testing?
notes.back: Black-box tests come from specifications and check behaviour; white-box tests come from internal structure and aim to cover it.
notes.explanation: They differ in the source of the tests, and so in what they are best at finding.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can the syllabus’s four test types be applied at every test level?
notes.back: Yes, all four can be applied at all test levels, although the focus differs at each level.
notes.explanation: Levels and types are separate dimensions, so every combination is possible.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester designs system tests so that every step in a loan-approval work flow is exercised. Can white-box testing be done at the system test level?
notes.back: Yes. All four test types can be applied at all test levels; here the structure covered is a work flow.
notes.explanation: White-box testing is not limited to code; the syllabus names work flows among the structures it uses.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.2 “Test Types”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus, what does confirmation testing confirm?
notes.back: That the fix really removed the original defect.
notes.explanation: Its question is narrow: is this particular defect gone?
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which confirmation testing option reuses existing tests?
notes.back: Executing all the tests that previously failed because of the defect.
notes.explanation: If the fix works, the tests that exposed the defect should now pass.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which confirmation testing option adds tests?
notes.back: Writing extra tests for whatever code was changed in making the fix.
notes.explanation: A fix can itself change code, and those changes need tests of their own.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When time or money is short, what might confirmation testing be restricted to?
notes.back: Exercising the steps that should reproduce the defect’s failure, and checking that the failure no longer occurs.
notes.explanation: This is the minimum that still answers whether the fix worked.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A defect meant that invoices with a zero amount crashed the print module. With a fix delivered and one hour left before release, what is the least the tester can do to confirm it?
notes.back: Repeat the steps that caused the crash and check it no longer happens
notes.choices:
A) Repeat the steps that caused the crash and check it no longer happens
B) Run the whole regression suite instead
C) Nothing; fixes do not need testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: regression testing looks for side effects elsewhere; it does not replace checking the fix itself. C: the syllabus says testing should include confirmation testing after a fix.
notes.explanation: Under time pressure, confirmation testing can shrink to reproducing the failure’s steps and checking it is gone.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus, what does regression testing confirm?
notes.back: That the change, even a fix that passed confirmation testing, has had no harmful side effects.
notes.explanation: Even a verified fix can still break something else.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where could the adverse consequences of a change show up?
notes.back: In the component that was changed, in other components of the same system, or even in other connected systems.
notes.explanation: Effects can spread well beyond the changed code, which widens where regression tests may be needed.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the syllabus advise doing before regression testing, and why?
notes.back: An impact analysis, to recognise how much regression testing is needed.
notes.explanation: Knowing which parts could be affected lets the team size the regression effort.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In maintenance, why may impact analysis be done before a change is made?
notes.back: To judge whether the change is worth making, given what it could affect elsewhere in the system.
notes.explanation: Here the analysis informs the decision itself, not just the testing that follows.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team must change how a shared date-formatting routine works and wants to know which screens and reports could be affected before planning regression tests. What should it do?
notes.back: An impact analysis
notes.choices:
A) An impact analysis
B) A retrospective
C) Confirmation testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: a retrospective reviews how the team worked, not which parts a change could affect. C: confirmation testing checks a fixed defect, and no defect is involved.
notes.explanation: Impact analysis maps which screens and reports the change could touch, and so how wide the regression testing needs to be.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why is regression testing a strong candidate for automation?
notes.back: The suites are rerun again and again, and they usually grow with every iteration or release.
notes.explanation: Repeated, growing work is where automation pays back most.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team’s manual regression suite has grown from 50 to 600 test cases over ten releases and is rerun before every release. What does the syllabus suggest?
notes.back: It is a strong candidate for automation.
notes.explanation: A suite that is run many times and keeps growing is exactly the case the syllabus describes.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between confirmation testing and regression testing?
notes.back: Confirmation testing checks that the fix removed the original defect; regression testing checks that the change caused no adverse effects elsewhere.
notes.explanation: They answer different questions about the same change, so one cannot replace the other.
notes.contrast: Did the fix work, versus did it break anything else.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After a fix for a defect that let users set a birth date in the future, a tester tries again to enter a future birth date. Which kind of testing is this?
notes.back: Confirmation testing
notes.choices:
A) Confirmation testing
B) Regression testing
C) Acceptance testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the tester is checking the fixed defect itself, not unchanged areas. C: acceptance testing is a test level about accepting the system, not re-checking one fix.
notes.explanation: Re-trying the behaviour that failed, to see whether the defect is gone, is confirmation testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After the birth-date fix, a tester reruns the existing tests for the unchanged registration, login and profile screens. Which kind of testing is this?
notes.back: Regression testing
notes.choices:
A) Regression testing
B) Confirmation testing
C) Component integration testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the tester is not re-checking the fixed defect but other areas. C: the purpose is to find side effects of a change, not to test interfaces between components as such.
notes.explanation: Checking that a change caused no adverse effects in unchanged parts is regression testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 30
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: At which test levels are confirmation and regression testing needed?
notes.back: At every test level where a defect is fixed or a change is made.
notes.explanation: Changes can happen at any level, so the change-related testing follows them there.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.2.3 “Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Testing a change to an operational system includes which two things?
notes.back: Evaluating whether the change was implemented successfully, and checking for regressions in the unchanged parts.
notes.explanation: A change can fail in itself or disturb the rest of the system.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A live library-loans system gets a new rule limiting renewals to three. Besides checking the new rule works, what else should its maintenance testing do?
notes.back: Check for regressions in the unchanged parts of the system.
notes.explanation: Most of the system is untouched, but it still has to be shown to work as before.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two categories of maintenance the syllabus mentions?
notes.back: Any two of: corrective; adaptive to changes in the environment; improving performance or maintainability.
notes.explanation: The syllabus points to a separate maintenance standard for the full detail.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two one-line changes are made to a live hospital system: one to a label colour, one to a drug-dose calculation. Which scope factor makes the second need far more testing?
notes.back: The degree of risk of the change.
notes.explanation: Both changes are the same size; what differs is how much harm a mistake could do.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the same live system, one release alters a single message text while another rewrites the whole billing module. Which scope factor most separates their testing needs?
notes.back: The size of the change.
notes.explanation: A bigger change touches more of the system and so calls for wider testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The same small change is made to a ten-screen booking app and to a national tax platform with thousands of screens. Which scope factor differs between them?
notes.back: The size of the existing system.
notes.explanation: A larger existing system has more unchanged parts that may need regression checks.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A planned enhancement adds contactless payment to a live parking-meter system. Which category of maintenance-testing trigger is this?
notes.back: Modification
notes.choices:
A) Modification
B) Upgrade or migration of the operational environment
C) Retirement
notes.choicesExplained: B: the software itself is enhanced; its platform is not moving. C: the system is not reaching the end of its life.
notes.explanation: The syllabus files planned enhancements, corrective changes and hot fixes under modifications.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council moves its live planning-applications system from its own servers to a cloud platform. Which category of maintenance-testing trigger is this?
notes.back: Upgrade or migration of the operational environment
notes.choices:
A) Upgrade or migration of the operational environment
B) Modification
C) Retirement
notes.choicesExplained: B: the change is to where the system runs, not to its features. C: the system carries on; it is not being withdrawn.
notes.explanation: Moving from one platform to another is the syllabus’s example of an environment migration.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A bank switches off an old savings-account system for good once all customers have moved to a new one. Which category of maintenance-testing trigger is this?
notes.back: Retirement
notes.choices:
A) Retirement
B) Modification
C) Upgrade or migration of the operational environment
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing is being enhanced or corrected. C: the old system is not moving platform; it is reaching the end of its life.
notes.explanation: An application reaching the end of its life is the syllabus’s retirement trigger.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Into which three categories does the syllabus classify triggers for maintenance and maintenance testing?
notes.back: Modifications; upgrades or migrations of the operational environment; retirement.
notes.explanation: Each describes a different reason an operational system changes.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What testing can an upgrade or migration of the operational environment require?
notes.back: Tests of the new platform and of the altered software, or, when data arrives from another application, tests that it converted correctly.
notes.explanation: Both the platform and the data may be new to the system after a move.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A gym chain imports ten years of member records from a rival chain’s software into its own live membership system. What kind of testing does the syllabus say this can require?
notes.back: Testing of the data conversion.
notes.explanation: Migrated data from another application must be shown to have been converted correctly.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When a system is retired, when can testing of data archiving be required?
notes.back: When long data-retention periods are required.
notes.explanation: If data must be kept for years after the system goes, the archive has to be trustworthy.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides archiving, what else may need testing when a system is retired?
notes.back: Restore and retrieval procedures after archiving, in case certain data is needed during the archiving period.
notes.explanation: An archive is only useful if the data can be got back out when needed.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A law firm retires its old case-management system but must keep closed case files for fifteen years and occasionally produce them for court. What should its retirement testing cover?
notes.back: Data archiving, plus the restore and retrieval procedures for archived data.
notes.explanation: Long retention calls for archive testing; the chance of needing files later calls for retrieval testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 2.3 “Maintenance Testing”, p. 31
